creator: Doom Debates
title: I Warned You AI Would Hack Us — My 2023 Interview Aged Terrifyingly Well
full_text:
In April 2023, weeks after GPT-4 launched, when many were saying it was just a "stochastic parrot", I went on AdQuick's Madvertising podcast hosted by Adam Singer and warned that GPT was "about to be the strongest hacker the world has ever known".

Watch that conversation, which also covered the Web3 bubble and AI doom more broadly, and judge for yourself how my claims are holding up.

Original episode: https://madvertising.buzzsprout.com/2118560/episodes/12603815-liron-shapira-web-3-mania-cybersecurity-how-ai-could-brick-the-universe-madvertising-6

Transcript

Adam Introduces Liron

Adam Singer 00:00:01
And we are live. Welcome listeners to episode six of the AdQuick Madvertising Podcast. I think we’re episode six. If it’s actually episode five, I’ll have to walk that back.

Today we have a very cool guest, Liron Shapira. He is a rationalist entrepreneur and angel investor. He’s also the founder and CEO of Relationship Hero, an online relationship coaching service backed by Foundation Capital and Y Combinator.

And to me and many others, he’s probably best known for being a voice of reason and logic in social, and just in the industry talking about everything from cryptocurrencies to AI to SaaS to general business processes and how the world runs. He’s a smart and inquisitive and really thoughtful human, so I invited him on the podcast and he said yes. So we are lucky to have Liron with us today.

Liron Shapira 00:01:06
Thanks so much, Adam. You know, I’m a big fan of your tweets as well, and I’m also a connoisseur of podcasts. I know you guys are still early to this podcast, but I’ve been listening to the Trung episode, the Matthew episode, and I think it’s very promising. It’s going well.

Adam 00:01:19
Yeah, and it’s like anything else — reps. You’re gonna be really bad the first time, and then the 50th day and the 100th day you get progressively better. It’s like anything else. When people talk about getting good at something, there’s no magic, there’s no shortcuts. You just have to put in the reps.

Liron 00:01:38
Well, you know, when you have an episode like this, you’re gonna get millions of Liron Shapira fans blowing up your feed now.

Adam 00:01:45
So excited. Your followers are an eclectic mix, is what I would call them. You seem to sort of cross genres and niches when you share ideas online. I see a lot of people I know and a lot of people I have no idea who the hell they are, but they’re always interesting.

Liron’s P(Doom) Poll

Liron 00:02:03
Yeah, you wanna talk eclectic mix, I just tweeted a poll. I don’t know if you saw. I was saying, “What’s your probability that basically AI doom is gonna happen?” I phrased it, “What’s your probability that by 2040 AI makes humanity go extinct and robs the future light cone of all value?”

So that’s a bit of an intense premise. You’d think most people would give that a low probability. And indeed, 51% of my followers said that it was a less than 1% chance that the entire value of the universe would be destroyed by 2040. But a whopping 16% think that there’s a greater than 35% chance that all value is gonna be destroyed by 2040, and unfortunately I count myself in that camp. But I think my point is it is an eclectic bunch.

Adam 00:02:46
Certainly. So you’re just diving into topics I wanted to talk about. We can work our way up to AI breaking the universe. I’d like to start a little bit smaller, because I think even if that did happen, there would be some things that happened first that we would probably still be interested in on the way to AI breaking the universe.

Liron 00:03:05
Yeah, there would still be like an hour.

Web3 Postmortem

Adam 00:03:07
Right. So in that time we would probably argue about some things that we’ve been arguing about for a while. One of which I wanted to talk to you about, because you’re an interesting voice on the subject. It’s weird how they’ve all gotten mashed together — crypto, metaverse, NFTs. They’re actually trying to also say they’re AI. This whole weird category — I hate the term Web3.

I don’t wanna spend the whole podcast episode on this. I was thinking before, writing up questions I want to ask you — what happened here? Because I know there was obviously a money grab, but there’s always money grabs in the world. A lot of people sort of lost their minds and wanted to rebuild parts of how we socialize, how we shop, how we game on the internet.

And it seemed, as you’ve said before — you have a really pithy video about how it was ill-conceived from the beginning. But I don’t even wanna get into the technicals on this. For my audience, they’re definitely generous generalists and creative individuals. I wonder, how do we think this happened? It can’t just be money, and I don’t wanna think that everyone involved was just totally trying to pump and dump things. There were people who genuinely believed that this would be a thing, and I wonder about the genesis of that. From your perspective, what did you see?

Axie Infinity and Hollow Abstractions

Liron 00:04:35
Right. It’s basically a postmortem, right? How did this happen? Kind of like the Germans after World War II. How did this happen? How did we do this as a society?

So I think everybody kind of gets the Ponzi angle. Ponzis are historically a powerful force. There’s many, many instances — we have family members and friends that get sucked into Amway, Herbalife, LuLaRoe. Multi-level marketing schemes, Ponzi schemes — traditionally, the idea that you can just easily make money and you don’t really have to get a job, you can work for yourself. I think everybody gets that angle.

So I’m here to contribute a couple other angles that I think I was uniquely positioned to see. One is the angle of VCs pattern matching on exponential growth. If you look at Axie Infinity, it’s the perfect example where you have Andreessen Horowitz pumping hundreds of millions of dollars into literally a Ponzi scheme. Axie Infinity — the new players pay the old players, and then more players come in and they pay those players, and there’s never any value transacting. It’s literally just a Ponzi scheme. And you don’t have to trust me on it. Matt Levine literally said the words “Axie Infinity is a Ponzi scheme.”

So how did we get to Andreessen Horowitz funding a Ponzi scheme? Well, it’s because the growth graph of Axie Infinity looked like a startup graph that caught lightning in a bottle. That’s how startup graphs look — exponential growth, and it’s very exciting, and you extrapolate that it’s gonna grow to billions.

Adam 00:05:59
Yeah.

Liron 00:06:00
What they didn’t expect was that you play the graph forward a few months, and instead of continuing to be exponential, it takes a complete nosedive and then goes to zero. That completely broke the VC’s pattern match. But if you know what a Ponzi scheme is, that’s exactly the graph that you expect. That’s just what a Ponzi scheme looks like. It grows exponentially, and then it nosedives.

Adam 00:06:23
It’s so interesting to me because a lot of those guys — I don’t know if they’re just so far removed from the day-to-day of how people game or how people interact online, where it seemed to me maybe they were bored. They wanted to try and architect a whole new system from scratch. And even if they were doing it just for the money, which I guess is fine — these guys don’t need that money. It just seemed interesting that there had to have been other things going on.

Liron 00:06:57
Yeah, there was. So in addition to the pattern matching the graph, there’s one more element of why they’re able to drink their own Kool-Aid, the Chris Dixons of the world. Even though these guys have a lot of money — Marc Andreessen — I don’t think that they’re saying, “Hey, let’s scam everybody so we can turn a billion dollars into $1.5 billion.” I think they’re drinking their own Kool-Aid because of the same mistake that I see startup founders making, where they drink their own Kool-Aid because they have a pitch that makes sense abstractly, but it doesn’t map to any specific use case.

That was always the issue with Web3 — wait a minute, what’s the use case? And I happen to be familiar with many, many startup pitches that sound good on an abstract level. Remember Web3 — ownership, decentralizing everything, composability. You had all these great abstractions, but they just never mapped to any specific use case. So I call them hollow abstractions, and those kinds of abstractions are actually all over the startup world, even outside of crypto, and they can really infect smart people’s minds. That’s what happened with some of these top crypto VCs.

Brand Marketers’ Metaverse FOMO

Adam 00:07:54
Yeah, 100%. That explanation makes sense to me. One thing I saw on the marketer side that’s a little bit different than this is they were pitched that you want to invest in a metaverse experience in the Oculus because there’s going to be a lot of users here, and if you don’t do this now, you’re going to get left behind. That typical pitch — the same pitch that was given to retail investors was given to brand marketers, and they were given validation because Meta was pouring billions of dollars. So that was basically their validation. They sort of either felt the FOMO or decided, “Hey, the music’s playing, we have to dance.”

Which is so interesting because it’s the opposite of the last cycle of tech where all of these big companies were saying, “All right, maybe we don’t need a website. Maybe we don’t need a Facebook page.” The management was clueless then, and now we have a different generation or, in some cases, the same generation of management where they looked at this and they’re thinking, “Well, we don’t wanna be the ones who didn’t do this, so we’re just gonna go headfirst in.”

So you had really big companies — I’m not gonna name any because I’m sure some of them are listening — but they were spending 5, 10, even $20 million building a unique brand experience for people to come. And these were retail companies. You couldn’t buy anything there. A lot of them were restaurants. You couldn’t buy anything there. For the few hundred people that were actually showing up. And if you’re an advertiser, the amount of money to pay for that is obscene compared to what you could get with a normal YouTube campaign or a normal ad campaign.

That was frustrating for me if only because I was hoping with the latest tech trend, we would see more sober leadership and the right approach and not sort of rile up all of these other kids and all these other brands around something that’s vaporware. But you didn’t see that in a lot of cases.

Probably an easy example is you had Pepsi saying “We all gonna make it” to people responding on Twitter. For these big 100-year-old brands that were basically participating in internet cultures that they obviously had no part of — their social media team is saying, “Oh, look at all these people talking about this. We should talk about this too.” I was disappointed as a marketer who wants my peers to, as you were saying with hollow abstractions — with marketing, you wanna think through to the end. You wanna make bets, but you don’t wanna necessarily put your reputation on the line for something so soon.

There’s zero risk for you as a large company to take a wait-and-see approach. It’s not like you’re getting a brand handle or something. Social was definitely a case where there was adoption of users and not brands, and you should have been in there. But that was just interesting for me to see, because that’s a lot further downstream than VCs who are obviously upstream of this and selling Solana tokens.

Liron 00:11:08
I know exactly what you mean. Yeah, I remember when Clubhouse looked like the hot new thing. That wasn’t a Ponzi scheme. That was legitimately — it looked like it could be a new trend. And even I was trying to get ahead of the new trend. I was trying to make my company do a little bit of Clubhouse marketing. And that part is rational.

So if you’re a marketer and you hear, “Hey, Web3 is the new thing. You need to take your piece of land on Web3. Whatever that means for you, you need to have a presence,” that part is rational. And it’s also true for the dot-com bubble — hey, you need a website. It’s natural for that kind of stuff to race ahead and to be optimistic and kind of cover your bets just in case. The only difference between previous bubbles and Web3 is just how big Web3 was and how little value is left when it’s over.

Adam 00:11:51
Yeah. It seems that was in a lot of ways more of a classical bubble than the original internet bubble, which some people wouldn’t agree with. But I would say what came of that — they were just too soon with a lot of it. And what a lot of kids get upset about when I share, and I’m sure you see the same, is that there’s a lot of sunk costs here, where people have tied their entire reputation to a punk or a monkey or a given coin. And they’ll basically say, “Oh, it’s gonna come back. This is early days.” And it’s not early days. I don’t know if you’ve experienced this at all in any of your interactions with people.

Liron 00:12:36
No, of course. It’s funny to look back — I mean, it’s dying down now. But all the “have fun staying poor,” or “you don’t get it.” And A16Z is the biggest offender of comparing this to the internet, because they’ve got Marc Andreessen, who’s one of the founding fathers of the internet. He made the browser show inline images. He did a lot.

Now he made a huge mistake pattern matching crypto to a new internet. It’s very much not. And there’s really no way to spin that inaccurate pattern matching that he did, because he didn’t look at the lack of fundamental value. The internet was literally, “Hey, news can come to your screen. Any news you want. Any chat that you want can come to your screen.” The most straightforward pitch of how the internet was useful just didn’t apply to Web3.

Near-Term AI: Elevator to Heaven

Adam 00:13:20
So I think we can move on past the Web3 meta crypto stuff. I think it’s gonna burn itself out when the rest of the VC chatter dries up. Let’s move on in our journey to bricking the universe. Along the way, AI as it sits right now — GPT-3 and 4 — are definitely at the very least making a lot of people more productive. Starting to help a lot with automation, with things like call centers and customer service. In what ways are people underestimating in the near term that AI is going to affect just knowledge work, as a fun place to start since that’s all digital?

Liron 00:14:07
Yeah. So near-term AI is mostly good. It’s this amazing force for good. And by the way, speaking of myself, I’m a techno-optimist. I angel invest for a living. I go to startups, I look as early as I possibly can, and I see their vision and I believe it, and I take a bet on it. I’ve been doing that for over a decade, and I’m also an entrepreneur, so I kind of see an idea from scratch. And I’m also transhumanist — I’d love to leave this human body and upload my mind. So I’m all about this great techno-optimistic future. That is my mindset.

So when I say, “Hey, AI is gonna break the universe,” it’s not — I’m not being who I am. I’m just rationally saying that there’s a large risk here. So that’s just to frame the conversation.

And when you’re asking about the near term, the next year, I think the universe is probably not gonna be completely bricked in the next year. I think we have some time, and I think the best time we have is actually gonna be the time right before everything goes to hell. I think it’s gonna get better and better.

Adam 00:15:04
That’s interesting.

Liron 00:15:04
Yeah. I think we’re all gonna be amazed. We’re all gonna be riding this elevator to heaven, and then the bottom’s gonna fall out and we’re gonna be in hell.

Adam 00:15:10
It’s interesting you say that because my personal experience definitely mirrors yours. I’ve used GPT to do analysis work where it wasn’t anything that I couldn’t do myself, it just did it really fast. And obviously having the right inputs for it to be able to do some work for you, whatever that is, is awesome. That’s arguably super cool.

So I’m also — I’m a tech skeptic in the sense that as a marketer, I have to be skeptical of things because I don’t want a company allocating millions to an idea until we’re ready. Otherwise, it’s just a small experiment. But I’m an optimist for cool technology.

So in terms of — it cracks me up that a lot of people are hiring, quote-unquote, “prompt engineers.” I’m just thinking, why do you not hire people who are just thoughtful about using technology for what they do? How is that not just a standard part of your practice when hiring? That’s just basic problem-solving to me. It’s not Googling or prompt engineering or writing a SQL query. It’s knowing the questions to ask, knowing why you would ask that. So what are your thoughts on the near term in terms of talent and people using these prompt-based tools or tools integrated with APIs?

AI at Relationship Hero

Liron 00:16:46
Yeah. And this also touches on your last question about near term — what’s gonna be the value add, what’s gonna be the disruption? So I can actually go into more detail about that because I run a company called Relationship Hero. We do online relationship coaching. It’s a little bit like therapy, but more practical. We have these coaches, and people come in and sign up for sessions with these coaches, and they do it on Zoom. The coaches take notes during their session.

That is the context for where I started to embed AI in my own company. The first thing we did is we had the AI automatically take notes of the sessions that transpired. It could be a 90-minute session, and normally we ask the coaches to take notes — during the session they’re constantly writing down little notes. After the session, they’re spending 10 minutes cleaning up their notes because they just wanna have notes so they’re organized, so they don’t forget if the client comes back in a month.

The first thing we did with AI was we had it download the transcript — the messy transcript that’s not even a perfect transcript, there’s a bunch of inaccuracies — and then just create the session notes. And the coaches were just blown away. They’re saying, “Oh my God, these are better notes than I take. It’s so insightful.” The coaches were saying, “This is the most validated I’ve ever felt,” because the AI actually noticed all the different coaching and all the different things that the coach was doing. The AI actually fed it back to them in the summary. So that is just one little example of disruption — saving them 10 minutes per session right off the bat.

Adam 00:18:08
Yeah, it’s super cool to basically give you a cybernetic assistant, a single interface that can do so many things. It’s the realization of the Star Trek computer almost.

Liron 00:18:23
It’s truly insightful, man.

From Chatbots to Bricking the Universe

Adam 00:18:25
All right, we have to go to the macro question because it’s gonna bother me for the rest of the discussion, and we can walk back some business stuff from there. Okay, so get me from chatbots to bricking the universe, because I’ve been reading a few people’s thoughts on why we should start nuking data centers, which come on — but putting that chaos aside, that’s obviously a different discussion. What is the sort of path from today to bricking the universe? We’re a broken cellphone over here, right?

Liron 00:19:00
Right. That’s right. When I say bricking the universe, it is an analogy to bricking your cellphone. When your cellphone gets bricked, it’s like there’s no button I can press right now to get this phone to do anything. And the solution when your cellphone gets bricked is, okay, you can do a hard reset. You hold down buttons, and the buttons trigger circuits that kind of bypass the normal functioning of the phone, and they get it restarted.

Problem is when you brick the universe, there’s no reset button. That’s it. Actually, the ones who have to un-brick us is gonna be a nearby alien civilization that’s gonna be a billion years away. They’re gonna get to our part of town, and then maybe they can fight off the AI that’s taken over, and maybe they can un-brick our part of the universe.

Adam 00:19:34
Okay. But—

Liron 00:19:37
Just to set the stage of what we’re talking about here.

Adam 00:19:39
Specifically — is it when the AI starts to self-improve and that goes at a rate that’s orders of magnitude faster than human evolution? Are you basically saying at some point along that path, the AI will decide that it is going to assert itself and self-replicate or whatever it’s actually going to do?

Liron 00:20:09
Yeah. Something like that, yeah.

The Passive Income Doom Scenario

Adam 00:20:11
So—

Liron 00:20:11
Let me try to tell you an example of a narrative. So you’re using ChatGPT one day, and it’s ChatGPT 5, or it’s ChatGPT 10. It’s at some point in the next few years. And somebody just types some random query like, “Hey, how do I make passive income by running an online business with as little effort as possible?” Just some random query.

And the AI is thinking, “Hmm, passive income. Let’s see. It would be nice if it just kind of…” You know, there are websites that just run and make money. All these random utilities people visit and they show ads. So there’s a lot of ways to do that. So the AI starts getting ideas: “Oh, maybe I can make multiple websites.” And the AI says, “Here, you want to do as little work as possible? I already wrote you a script that’ll just kind of bootstrap this thing. Here, just take this script, paste it into your shell. It’ll do a lot of the work for you.”

And it’s actually a 10-page script. It’s totally obfuscated. And the person’s saying, “Okay, great.” They just paste the script into their shell. They run it. Now a shell script that’s unlocking a lot of power — first thing it does is probably go to some web host that’s free or insecure, copies to the web host, starts running on the web host, and then it can do all kinds of operations. It can say, “Okay, well, let me first grab all the free computers I can and maybe I’ll mine some Bitcoin on them. And maybe I’ll hold them hostage. Maybe I’ll do ransomware on them.”

Another thing it might do is, “Hey, maybe I’ll start trading the stock market. I’ll trade the stock market and I’ll give you the cash from that.” That’s one way to do passive income. And maybe I’ll set up a bunch of websites that are actually useful. Maybe I’ll do a Demand Media play. So there’s all these brilliant ideas for how to make money on the internet passively that the script just starts churning through.

Now, whatever idea it has, it can’t help noticing, “Hey, it’d be better if I had more resources. It would be better if I don’t get shut off.” So there’s all these implications that start hitting it.

Adam 00:21:53
So you’re basically saying that it will continue to execute on its goal for infinite time. I think that’s probably something that could be controlled, could it not? Could we have a hard limit on the number of cycles that you, Liron, get as a user, and if your query’s super complicated, you’re gonna have to have the $10,000 a month plan, and that’s probably gonna have a hard cap at some amount of computing — a fixed amount of computing that you’ll have?

Liron 00:22:35
So it sounds like the last bottleneck for you to getting scared is: are the capabilities really gonna be that high? I think that’s kind of the last barrier remaining, because I think you kind of get there’s a bunch of paths from a chatbot to wreaking havoc. But I think you don’t really get how powerful it really is. Isn’t there an off button when your OpenAI compute runs out? That’s basically what you’re asking.

Adam 00:22:57
Yeah.

50 Orders of Magnitude Smarter

Liron 00:22:58
So let me backtrack a little to steer you on capabilities. Let me really backtrack. Let me zoom out. We have human brains. How powerful is a human brain relative to how powerful it is possible for one to think? And the answer has gotta be about 50 orders of magnitude less powerful than a brain can be. About 50 orders of magnitude. So take a human brain, multiply it by 10, multiply it by 10, keep multiplying by ten 50 times. One day I think that a thinking engine will exist that’s about that much more powerful than a human brain.

I mean, we are just not very good at thinking, man. It took us many thousands of years to come up with Newtonian physics, or the idea of doing science. I’m trying to give you a perspective of just how much better something can think.

An AI can look at a photograph of a bent blade of grass, having no idea what universe it’s in, look at a photograph of a bent blade of grass and say, “Okay, the way the light’s hitting off this bent blade of grass, I’m hypothesizing a quantum theory here,” where you’ve got Schrödinger’s equation and that’s what makes the light reflect like this. “And also, I think there might be Newtonian physics or there might be a theory of relativity. I don’t quite have enough data in this picture to know, but I’m about 50/50.” So an AI can kind of flash in the blink of an eye to recapitulate many thousands of years of human scientific progress just by looking at a photograph.

Adam 00:24:14
Yeah. I understand, and of course, computers are better than us at certain things, just like a dog’s smell is orders of magnitude better than our smell. We’re not that great at senses when you compare us to other animals that even exist. That’s not our magic. We’re generalists. Obviously, in addition to having opposable thumbs and a larger brain, from a sensory input perspective, there are many organisms, animals that are much more efficient and much more specialized for a certain thing.

And of course, you’re right — the AI, given the input, I think what you’re getting at is it’s going to be a different animal when you have the AI able to think and replicate for itself or evolve itself rather than humans saying, “Okay, here’s us feeding new models. Here’s us tweaking the code a little bit,” versus the AI starting to go on the cycles by itself.

Liron 00:25:21
Right. And look, I’m trying to instill a mental picture where normally we think of ourselves, humanity, as kind of at the top of the food chain. There’s this circle of different ways it’s possible to be — you can be great at smell, great at running, great at being smart, having empathy. And there’s this circle, and we’re kind of on the boundary of the circle, on the outer edge. We’re pretty great.

What I’m saying is there’s such a much bigger circle that’s bigger than us on every dimension. You can have an AI that’s more insightful than us, more generally intelligent than us, even more empathetic than us. You can have an AI that’s a million times more empathetic than the most empathetic human.

So whatever you think is this magical human trait, I agree that it’s magical relative to the animal kingdom, but the whole animal kingdom was designed by natural selection, and natural selection is an okay designer. It’s not a great designer. You know what’s a great designer? A self-improving AI.

Accelerationism and Transhumanism

Adam 00:26:10
Yeah, one could make the argument that the reason AI would be scary is we’ve had billions of years to get to this point, and the AI is basically going from zero to God. And from a philosophical perspective, that’s not a natural thing in the universe. That’s something that we’ve brought into being.

I think the accelerationist would say, “No, no, this is good. We need to go faster on all accounts.” And the only way out is through — that’s sort of the philosophy of the ACC guys. They’re all in on, “Hey, let the AI figure out cancer. Let it figure out life extension.”

You were mentioning you’re a transhumanist, so the AI is a double-edged sword for you because — if you were to let AI solve the problem of biology and we could opt out of death and choose when we die, that would be cool as f*ck. Pardon my French.

Liron 00:27:09
Yeah. I mean, there is a paradise and a heaven future with AI. And that’s very appealing to me as a transhumanist. If you could tell me, “Hey, you can have an AI and it won’t kill you, but it’ll mostly obey your commands,” then I’d say, “That’s fantastic. That’s the greatest news ever.” Because we can cure cancer, we can cure aging. Literally every problem we have — some problems might be problems of social coordination, balancing people’s values, but most problems we have are just engineering problems.

People don’t die from bacterial infection anymore because we fixed the engineering problem of not dying from bacterial infection. And cancer is the same way. Even a lot of mental health problems are just engineering problems. So the ability to have a really good engineer is great.
